MR. NOWLAN-STATEMENTS TO NEWSPAPER COLUMNIST BY MARC LALONDE RESPECTING CYC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege regarding a newspaper report yesterday in the Toronto Telegram based on an interview between Mr. Douglas Fisher, a part-time columnist, and Marc Lalonde, a full-time public servant. The subject matter of the interview was the operation of the Company of Young Canadians.
I believe this point involves the privileges of members of this House and, more specifically, the workings of the committee of the House which is studying this very subject matter. At one time it was requested that the list of witnesses include the said Marc Lalonde and that he appear before the committee in his capacity at that time as ViceChairman of the Provisional Council of the Company of Young Canadians. He happened also to be in the Prime Minister's office then. Some members thought his evidence would not be too relevant, and as the result of a motion that was passed, with some division of opinion, his name was struck off the list of witnesses and the said Marc Lalonde did not appear before the committee.
After a quick perusal of the article of which I gave you notice, Mr. Speaker, I find it sets out in very clear detail, in the question and answer form followed by Mr. Fisher and Mr. Lalonde, a number of comments on specific points which relate directly to the subject matter the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts has been studying. These comments also relate to the report of that committee which is at present being drafted and has been leaked to the press piecemeal yesterday and today, and perhaps again tomorrow.
It is very clear in the latter part of the article that Mr. Lalonde made certain statements which are in conflict wi.h a good deal of the evidence presented to the committee. In view of the fact that this committee of the House is supposed to bring forward a report on Friday based on the facts, it is only proper and reasonable that the said Marc Lalonde, having conversed with this newspaper columnist, should appear before the committee in order that it may clarify the implica ions in his remarks. The committee is supposed to make judgments and decisions based on the facts.
Perhaps questions of privilege are abused. I do not point to any particular rule that justifies my remarks today, but I think it is passing strange that a part-time journalist should get together with a full-time public servant to discuss a subject matter which a committee is currently considering. For that reason and that reason alone I feel there is an elementary question of privilege.
Because of our rules and because the committee is now sitting in camera writing its report, perhaps Your Honour, as the number one Commoner and the man to whom I appeal, has very little discretion in this matter unless I propose a motion to refer it to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. This whole affair seems to me to be a travesty on our committee system. Surely this is true when a man of the public eminence and authority that some people ascribe to Mr. Lalonde makes comments of this nature. I am not saying he had anything to do with the committee's decision not to call him. He may well have wanted to appear before the committee, and it may well be that he might have added relevant facts. But surely he should not discuss this matter for the purpose of a newspaper article at the very time the committee is writing its report.
Quite frankly, I am not sure whether I should move a motion to refer this matter to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. I am not sure when the committee's report is likely to be tabled in the House, but I understand it may be tabled on Friday. In any event, we find ourselves in an impossible position.
December 3, 1969

Company of Young Canadians
I wanted to bring this matter to Your Honour's attention. I know you cannot request Mr. Lalonde to attend the committee, but that is what should be done because this public servant is closely associated with Privy Council matters and is also very actively involved in other matters. For this reason I suggest he should not converse with columnists about subject matters being considered by committees of the House. Had this happened a week ago I am sure the committee might have reversed itself and asked him to appear and give evidence about the financial control he alleges was exerted.
I have almost concluded my remarks, Mr. Speaker. I fail to understand how progress can be made by exercising leadership, if the leadership is removed as suggested by the article. Such public discussion of a subject matter being considered by a committee of the House is almost tantamount to a travesty of the workings of that committee.

Mr. Speaker, I thought it might be helpful to hon. members if I made a statement concerning the business of the House for the period between now and the Christmas adjournment.
We have proposed that the House should rise for the Christmas adjournment on Friday, December 19. On this basis there would remain 13 sitting days for public business, including today. Two of these days are opposition days. Since they must be dealt with before December 10 it is our intention to call the opposition days on Monday and Tuesday of next week, December 8 and 9.
It is important that the following bills be finally disposed of before the adjournment because of the urgency of time in each particular case: Bill C-2 with regard to the Judges Act, which is urgent because of the necessity to add to the bench as soon as possible; Bill C-7 with regard to the Canadian National Railways, which is the annual financing bill of Canadian National Railways; Bill C-8, in respect of the Children of War dead (Education Assistance) Act; Bill C-139 in respect of the Income Tax Act; Bill C-155 in respect of the Excise Tax Act; Bill C-157 with regard to provisional payments for unthreshed grain; Bill S-8 in respect of loan companies and Bill S-9 in respect of trust companies. By way of explanation I should indicate that since the latter two bills expand the power of financial institutions to lend

Mr. Speaker, some 30 per cent of water pollution in Canada is caused by the phosphate content of detergents. speakeroldname: Mr. Gerard Loiselle (Parliameniary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
1. In the
course of reconstructing lock number 36 at Newboro and lock number 13 at Black Rapids, the Department of Transport has installed electrically-activated hydraulic lock machinery. The Department proposes to take no further initiatives of this sort until such time as these improvements have been thoroughly evaluated.
2.	Departmental officials have been making a continuing study of lock rehabilitation, reconstruction and operating procedures with assistance from the National Capital Commission and the National and Historic Parks Branch of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and in consultation with the Government of Ontario and other interested parties.
3.	The Department's plan contemplates that a particular lock should be reconstructed at such time as the lock is deemed to have reached imminent failure. The two locks referred to hereover were reconstructed on this basis. If experience warrants and if such a course of action seems justified, electrically-activated hydraulic lock machinery will be installed in other locks when reconstruction becomes necessary.
4.	It is postulated that 30 locks will require reconstruction at some time in the next 30 years. Estimated cost is $500,000 per lock,

of which $25,000 would be earmarked for electrically-activated hydraulic lock machinery (were same to be installed).
5.	No expenditures in this category are planned for the fiscal years 1969-70 and 197071.
6.	Existing "man-powered" lock machinery does not meet federal and provincial safety standards. Modifications to correct deficiencies would alter the general appearance and the essential character of much of this machinery. In the light of safety requirements, experience to date (at Black Rapids, in particular) suggests that the historical and scenic values inherent in the Rideau Canal System will be protected and enhanced if electrically-activated hydraulic lock machinery is properly designed and put in place and operated with due regard for aesthetic considerations.
7.	The Department is most intent upon protecting and enhancing what the Department recognizes as being a unique national asset and will continue to consult and to receive representations from all those who have an interest in the Rideau Canal System: meanwhile, Departmental studies continue.
8.	All canal structures have been rebuilt once or twice. The rehabilitation and recon-siruction program is a part of the Department's normal operating and maintenance program. No cost-benefit analysis of the Rideau Canal System has been undertaken.

subtopic: EXPULSION OF FRANK SHEER FROM CAMEROON
EXPULSION OF FRANK SHEER FROM CAMEROON
speechtext:
West):
1.	Was a Canadian citizen, Frank Sheer, resident of Ottawa, recently expelled from Cameroon by the authorities of that country and under what circumstances?
2.	What assistance, leading to release from arrest and confinement, was provided by the Canadian Charge d'Affaires, Marc Perron, at Yaounde?
3.	What protests were made to the Cameroonian Government by Canadian authorities concerning the abusive police treatment received by Mr. Sheer and what was the answer?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXPULSION OF FRANK SHEER FROM CAMEROON
speechtext:
1. Yes. Canadian citizen, Frank Sheer, a resident of Ottawa, on an assignment for International Color Film in Cologne, was expelled from Cameroon by the authorities of that country on November 1, 1969 following the expiry of his visa. Mr. Sheer was detained on October 27 near Ba-menda, West Cameroon, taken to Buea on October 28 and transferred by Federal Security Forces to Yaounde on October 31. Cameroonian authorities held him for interrogation on grounds of engaging in suspicious activities.

Although the region where Mr. Sheer was detained was a long way from the border between Cameroon and Nigeria, the Cameroonian Security Forces' suspicions appear to have been aroused as a result of Mr. Sheer travelling in that region carrying photographic equipment and wearing a bush jacket and haversack similar to those used by Cameroonian soldiers.
2.	Mr. Sheer's detention was brought to the attention of the Canadian Embassy by the British Vice-Consul at Buea as soon as he was aware of the situation. The Canadian Charge d'Affaires, succeeded in obtaining Mr. Sheer's release from detention and in arranging for him to stay in a hotel overnight in Yaounde prior to his departure from the country on November 1.
3.	In his conversation with the Canadian Charge d'Affaires, Mr. Sheer made no reference to physical abuse at the hands of Cameroonian police authorities.
The Canadian Charge d'Affaires in Yaounde has, however made representations to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs regarding their security forces' refusal to permit Mr. Sheer to contact a Canadian representative and their failure to inform the Canadian Embassy of the detention of Mr. Sheer.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. Burton), to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the tremendous increase in profits reported yesterday by all of Canada's chartered banks, and the need to consider imposing regulations to limit interest rates and other service charges.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 FINANCE INCREASE IN BANK PROFITS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Waterloo has proposed to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 in the circumstances to which he has just referred. The purpose of the proposed motion is to give this House an opportunity to debate the need to consider imposing regulations to limit interest rates and other service charges.
I must bring to the attention of hon. members that the House itself, by an order adopted October 30, empowered the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs to consider the present level of interest rates. Thus the very problem raised by the hon. member is specifically before a standing committee by order of the House. This would seem to indicate that this is the type of situation that, in spite of the circumstances explained by the hon. member, ought not to be the subject of an emergency debate

under Standing Order 26. In the circumstances I have to rule that the motion cannot be put to the House at this time.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell), to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the statement by the President of the Public Service Alliance of Canada on behalf of 140,000 public employees citing deteriorating relations between the staff unions and Treasury Board on a number of important issues, but most especially the absence of meaningful bargaining on the government's part and the "incredibly slow pace" of current negotiations.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: RELATIONS BETWEEN STAFF UNIONS AND TREASURY BOARD-PACE OF BARGAINING
speechtext:
The hon. member for Peace River sent me notice of his proposed motion in accordance with Standing Order 26, section (2). Since receiving the hon. member's notice I have had an opportunity to consider the subject matter of the topic which he proposes to raise on a motion to adjourn the House. As has often been said by the Chair in this session and as is repeated in the Standing Order, the question to be determined by the Chair is not the importance of the subject matter but rather the urgency of debate. Perhaps it might be helpful once again to quote the Standing Order and particularly subsection (16)(a) which reads as follows:
The matter proposed for discussion must relate to a genuine emergency, calling for immediate and urgent consideration.
There is no doubt in my mind that the relationship between the government and its employees is a matter of particular importance, but I cannot bring myself to feel that the continuing process of bargaining and negotiating is of such immediate urgency as to require the setting aside of the ordinary public business which the House will consider today. In the circumstances the motion proposed by the hon. member should not be put to the House.

The House resumed from Tuesday, December 2, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gray that Bill C-7, to authorize the provision of moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways system and Air Canada for the period from the 1st of January, 1969, to the 30th day of June, 1970, and to authorize the guarantee by Her Majesty of certain securities to be issued by the Canadian National Railway Company and certain debentures to be issued by Air Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS, AIR CANADA PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night when the House rose I was discussing the problem of transportation and the thousands of cars that were travelling from the Georgian Bay area-I notice in Hansard it is shown as "Thunder Bay" when it should be "Georgian Bay"-to Toronto and the general Lake Ontario area to the west and the east. I pointed out that there would be roughly well over one million people going to work morning and night using motor cars which carry from one to four or five people, each of these cars spewing out poisonous gas from their exhausts.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
When one considers, as I stated last night, that this is the industrial heartland of Canada and that almost one third of the federal income tax comes from that area, one realizes that not only is it a very important area but also becoming a congested one. With the density of the population increasing, by the year 2,000, according to the statisticians and the information that we have received, the area will be almost solidly built-up from Lake Ontario to Georgian Bay.
I do not believe that we are looking at this matter in proper realistic fashion. As I said before, there are numerous railway lines and roads going out of Toronto. Paralleling one another there is highway 400, highway 27 and highway 11 going north, and going west there is highway 401 and several other highways. Again, paralleling those are the railway lines. All we have to do is to think for a minute of
December 3, 1969
1556	COMMONS
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada the problem which, according to some people, is the greatest problem confronting us today, namely the problem of pollution, particularly air pollution.
You will see hanging over our cities great clouds of air pollution-Toronto is a good example. Every one of the cars that travel along the roads contributes to the pollution. A great many of these cars are used by people who go to work in Metropolitan Toronto. Anyone who has had the experience of travelling in the rush hour in Toronto will know that it takes just about as long to get out to the city limits as it does to travel over the next 60 miles. There is a congestion of cars travelling at a snails pace, pouring out poisonous gases which form a cloud over our city.
I say that the government today is very lax in bringing out a Canada water act and not bringing forth a Canada air pollution act. All you have to do is to drive into those cities and look them over. You will find a great cloud handing over them because all the poisonous gases rise up and form an umbrella. Then, condensation takes place, a fog forms over the area and finally comes down. I say to the government that the railway companies are derelict when they allow the abandonment of railway service, thus forcing people to use their cars to a greater extent to go to and from work, causing more congestion on the roads. This is the age of automation and of motor car travel. Very shortly this area will become so polluted we will have to devise ways and means to get all these people to work so that not only the whole city but surrounding area will not be poisoned as it is now to the point where many respiratory diseases such as emphysema are on the increase. Air pollution also contributes to many other respiratory diseases and may play a significant role in others.
The hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Cadieu) made a very moving speech on behalf of his constituents. As he pointed out, the railway officials have been derelict in not listening to the people who live in that area. The same thing is occurring in the area to which I have drawn the attention of the House. Not only does it include Toronto but also the Hamilton area, and I am surprised that some hon, members on the other side of the House have not spoken on this subject because it certainly concerns them also.
Members of the provincial: legislature are concerned about the matter, such as the member for Simcoe Centre and the member for Simcoe: East. I believe also that the hon.
[Mr. Rynard.l

member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Roberts) was one of those who took a train ride on the Go-Go Special which proved very conclusively that this train can be run at a profit. I am saying that railroad specialists have been hypocritical and the government has been derelict in allowing the railways to abandon railway lines, thus allowing the atmosphere to be polluted because more people are forced to use their cars to get to work. As the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) indicated, this area may very well be the site of a new airport which will add to the pollution of the area and to traffic congestion. In addition, in the four summer months many tourists come to the area, bringing with them thousands and thousands of dollars to spend in Canada. They come in in their motor cars, further polluting the air and adding to traffic congestion and traffic accidents.
Surely, something can be done to provide better service for people in that area. For example, the Northland Railroad could be utilized for this purpose. I have here in my hand a document entitled "The Ride of the Go-Go Special; a Test Run for Commuter Service". The railways are saying that this service is not economical and they are dissuading people from using it. They do not provide good service on it and they do not invite us to use it, nor are they trying to make things comfortable for passengers. In fact, it is just the opposite. I want to say to the House that this particular service pays its way. A test run was made at the expense of private individuals to prove that it could be run efficiently and economically, that in this way air pollution could be cut down, and that in the long run it would save the government millions of dollars in expense besides giving a worthwhile service. I warn the government that sooner or later they will have to take steps to combat air pollution in this area. They already have to do it in London and in other congested areas.
The results of the test run are very interesting. The total gross profit from the run amounted to $892. At one time transportation was the right of the people. Here is a service that pays for itself. I say that if the federal government and the provincial government, if necessary, do not co-operate to control air pollution, and traffic congestion they will be derelict in their duty and the people should force them to take action.
I should like to conclude by saying that since this service has been tested at the expense of private individuals and not with
December 3, 1969

government funds, it is a proven method of transportation which people will use-if given the opportunity and proper service-and will be meeting and dealing effectively with the problems of tomorrow. You, Mr. Speaker, know that to drive a motor car costs about 15 cents a mile. These people can ride to work on the railroad for approximately three cents a mile. They will use such a service, and it will cut down on the pollution on which, sooner or later, the government must take action. It has already taken action by means of the Canada Water Act; the next thing will be a Canada air pollution act.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the powers that be in transportation had better take a long look at their methods of discontinuing passenger lines, and giving poorer and poorer service so that the public will not use the remaining lines. The people have a right to expect better than this. The government should immediately get busy before we have a huge problem that will cost us millions of dollars to solve.
Look at the water pollution that we have now. We are suffering millions of dollars of loss because of it. We do not know yet what our losses will be because of air pollution. I conclude by saying that the Department of Transport and the government had better get busy and examine their policy with respect to the closing of railway lines and the calling of services and the cutting of services.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to belabour this debate on Bill C-7, but since the bill was first presented I have received a large number of letters and telegrams from people, particularly in Edmonton and the surrounding areas, who are going to be affected by the elimination of passenger service in Canada. At this time I would like to read into Hansard two press releases. The first is a press release from a meeting of the members of railway unions on the elimination of CNR trains Nos. 5 and 6, the "Panorama", held in Edmonton on November 14, 1969. I quote:
The elimination of Canadian National Railways trains No. 6 and No. 5, the "Panorama" has been the subject of a meeting held in Edmonton today attended by representatives and members of Railway Labour Unions and others concerned with a loss of important railway transportation service to communities, towns and cities across the country.
At a time when the matter of public transportation is being given intense scrutiny in order to determine the requirements of the travelling public
DEBATES	1557
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada an important service is to be dropped increasing the burden on remaining available transportation facilities which are in turn in the process of being considered for abandonment.
A large number of railway employees with up to ten or more years of service will be laid off increasing the number of unemployed in our city. As an example: the number of employees in Edmonton actually operating the trains to be eliminated numbers 40. Add to this all of those involved in other departments and the numbers are substantial.
All of the railway employees involved are members of a community who works to provide service to their community making them more than just employees and it is because of this fact that we met today to ask other members of the community to question the whole matter of transportation in order to determine what direction it is headed.
We urge our fellow citizens to write to their members of parliament, to ask questions of those whose responsibility it is to provide them with a decent way to go from one place to another and to request that investigation be continued by appropriate committees as to just what is happening to the public transportation dollar.
Subsidization of public services is an accepted fact. They must be maintained in the interest of the public good and well-being. Railway service is the only available means of transportation which a great number of Canadians can afford to use and it is incumbent upon the country to provide it.
We request those who use our railways to join us in protesting elimination of services in a haphazard manner. It is a loss to their way of life; it is a loss of our livelihood.
The second press release is titled, "Incredible Canadian." It is an article by an outstanding columnist on the Edmonton Journal, Art Evans. I quote:
-another "Incredible Canadian" is in the news.
I refer to the CPR's transcontinental "name train" which the company claims lost $19.6 million in 1968.
The figure may be accurate but it seems incredible in view of the tales one has heard about requests for space being turned down because none was available. These gave me the impression that The Canadian was doing a brisk business.
This impression was supported on several occasions last summer when I had an opportunity to watch The Canadian pass through Calgary. There were faces looking out from every window but perhaps they were only painted on to conceal the sad truth that, inside, the train was practically empty except for crew members. In fairness to the company I must admit that I was only a trackside watcher and did not actually walk through the coaches counting "real" passengers. And so it is entirely possible that my impression of The Canadian as a busy carrier was quite mistaken.
Still, if all those faces at the window were real and represented flesh-and-blood passengers, an operating loss of close to $20 million does seem somewhat on the high side. One is curious to know every detail of the costing formula applied.

For example it would not be fair to charge against The Canadian the cigars smoked by William Van Horne during the building of the railway, or the refreshments (if any) served at the last spike ceremony in 1885. It is not suggested such charges are included in The Canadian's operating costs but official assurance on this point would be welcomed by the public.
Presumably, Canada's Transportation Commission will closely examine passenger loss figures submitted by the railways in applications to abandon certain services. What follows next should be determined by the commission's findings.
I have many other letters of protest here. One is from John L. Pickett, Secretary-Treasurer local 861 of the United Transportation Union. There is one from Mr. Ralph Dent, President, Brotherhood Railway Carmen of the United States and Canada. There is another from Mr. English, Executive Secretary of the Edmonton and District Labour Council I could read quite a few of these letters into the record, Mr. Speaker.
Obviously what is happening is that the government is hiding behind the CNR. The government should simply tell the CNR that it will not allow essential rail services to be cut. Instead, the government is washing its hands, taking the attitude that it is none of its business. What of the people of this country? What of the many hundreds, even thousands in western Canada, deprived of rail service because of the government's failure? We have had the same story from the government for too long. To hear this government, it has no control over anything.
A few days ago the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) appeared before a committee and said the government had no control over the Company of Young Canadians. The government has no control over the CBC. The only thing the government makes any effort to control is the press. It set up a committee to do that. As we heard today, the government has no control over Devco. The government has cut itself off from reality. Recently, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) went out to the mountains and delivered himself of some observations on genetics of the future. He said humans would be produced in the same way as chickens are produced. I feel my hon. friend from Huron would be a greater expert than the Prime Minister in that respect.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
This statement is not surprising since the Prime Minister views the taxpayers as so many chickens. His government has been plucking them like chickens for some time.


He said his party was a supermarket of ideas. At times it sounded more like a bargain basement.
These projected rail cuts have aroused a great deal of resentment in western Canada. I want to call the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) to a statement made by D. N. Secord, Secretary-Treasurer of the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway, Transport and General Workers. He is a union official and represents a great many of the people who will suffer if the CNR goes ahead with these cuts. He said, and I quote from the Ottawa Citizen of November 11:
It is folly even to consider such drastic cuts in train passenger runs at a time when our highways and airways are becoming dangerously overcrowded.
Surely, the government must be aware of this. I am one of those who, on occasion, has seen fit to register complaints about air service both east and west to and from Edmonton. Now, the CNR is going to make the situation worse by reducing rail service.
At times it is almost impossible to get accommodation either by rail or by air. Certainly, this is no time to be cutting out essential passenger service. As Mr. Secord pointed out, the CNR logged over 2,000,000 passenger miles last year. Surely, the Minister of Transport is aware that even a small part of this load would bog down the airlines completely. After all, he has his Newfoundland Bullet, why should he deprive western Canada of service?
For far too long the CNR and the CPR both have made these decisions in their own interests, rather than in the interests of the affected taxpayers. It is time the government stepped in and asserted its authority. The answer is, of course, that the CNR wants to reserve the railways for more profitable freight traffic because they feel passengers can be transported more cheaply by bus. Since the railways generally have a piece of the bus lines, they cannot lose.
As far as the public is concerned, the railways are still echoing Commodore Vanderbilt's remark: "The public be damned." He was a railway magnate, also. But times have changed, and the people in this country have some rights. They are not going to be deprived of essential services by high-handed railway decisions. Transportation and communication are two of the most essential services in a modern state. I point out to the minister that this steady cannibalization of rail services is going to end in disaster.
December 3, 1969

The elimination of essential lines serving a major metropolitan area like Edmonton is a slap in the face to one of Canada's major cities and a blow to development. When British Columbia came into the Dominion in 1871, one of the conditions was the establishment of essential rail services within ten years. Now, the CNR is attempting to whittle away at services at a time when growing population and shipping demands must be met.
The railways remain Canada's principal means of transportation and retain a crucial role in opening up new areas. An example was the 400-mile Pine Point Railway opened in 1964, opening up a rich new copper and zinc find for processing and distribution. The 230-mile Alberta Resources Railway is another example where public confidence in the country's future spurred the building of new facilities.
In 1966, the railways moved 41 per cent of Canada's freight, compared to 9.4 per cent moved by trucks. Surely, they are getting their share of freight haulage. The less lucrative passenger lines have been steadily removed. In 1966, for example, the railways moved only 3.9 per cent of passenger traffic, compared to 84 per cent moved by automobile, 5.3 per cent moved by bus and 6.5 per cent moved by air. When you look at the human factor, and this is something the railways seem to forget, you find that the railways employ 150,000 Canadians; they have a $1 billion payroll; they have revenues of $1| billion and they have expenses of $1.4 billion.
When you look at passenger and freight service in terms of volume, you find that in 1960 the railways carried 158 million tons; in 1968, they carried 224 million tons; in 1960, they carried 19 million passengers, and in 1968, they carried 22.5 million passengers. The picture, then, is a constant expansion on the freight hauling side and a moderate expansion in passengers. But even so, surely with 22.5 million passengers, that traffic cannot be a total loss. As far as can be seen from the figures, the railways are taking more and more out of the country and putting less and less back in.
One hundred years ago, they promised they would take Canadians for a ride-they are still taking Canadians for a ride! It is time the government stepped in and laid down the law to these autocratic power barons with singletrack minds. We have a railway Tsar in this country and the Minister of Transport is the Tsarovich, that is the son of a Tsar. The Tsar
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada is a former government minister, the former member for Bonavista-Twillingate, whose memory has been overshadowed by the achievements of the present member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan).
Why does not the government call on the chairman of the Transport Commission to exercise the enormous and autocratic powers they gave him? The time has come to enforce a square deal for Canadians-not a square wheel, such as we have been getting. I say to the minister through you, Mr. Speaker, act now!

subsubtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS, AIR CANADA PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had really no intention of taking part in this debate until I heard the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski). I want to say to you and the members of the House that I agree almost completely with what he said.
I would just remind members of this House, in talking about the railway situation in Canada, that a hundred years ago there was a fellow by the name of Sir John A. Macdonald who united this Canada of ours by building not one, but two, railways from Halifax to Vancouver. He did not have the money to do this nor did he have the machinery, but he went ahead and did it just the same. Today, in my opinion, the leaders of our railways are tearing up those lines. Mr. Speaker, that is not the way I would develop Canada. I agree whole-heartedly that there are two sides to the question. I agree we cannot continually carry lines that lose money on a day to day basis. On the other hand, I think there is a half way measure that railway leaders should accept.
One of the things the leaders should accept is a deal made 100 years ago which has been renewed many times. This deal was a two way street with the government giving so much and the railways agreeing to give so much. I think the government-otherwise the people of Canada-have held up their end of the bargain but I am not at all sure that the Presidents of the Canadian National Railways and the Presidents of the Canadian Pacific Railway kept their end.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I know as an absolute fact that in many small areas in the province of Ontario certain documents were signed many years ago. When I say "many", I mean 40 or 50. In these documents the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways guaranteed service to particular towns or villages as long as the waters
1560	COMMONS
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada went down the creek, as long as the moon shone, or whatever it may be. In return the railways received several thousands of dollars from the municipalities concerned in order to have the railway lines go through. Now I say, Mr. Speaker, that if the Canadian National Railways or the Canadian Pacific Railway is going to stop this service they had better think about repaying some of that money.

We have their signatures right on the line. Governments can change, and policies can change but as far as the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways are concerned, documents signed 50 years ago should be good today. I do not think they are doing a very good job.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
A moment ago I said that some railway lines in Canada must be abandoned. Operations over them must cease, as we all agree. Many such lines have already been abandoned. Nevertheless, as representatives of the people of Canada we have the obligation of telling the government that the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific should abide by their obligations. The railways were a party to the contracts and we, members of Parliament who represent various constituencies in this country, are under the obligation of telling the government that our two major railways have not done at all badly. One, in particular, which is privately owned and works on a free enterprise basis, has not done at all badly. I say this in a kindly way because I appreciated the speech the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) made yesterday. I think he made an outstanding oration and put before us many outstanding facts which those of us who have not been here as long as others were glad to hear.
I think the government and the heads of the railway companies would do well to heed his observations.
May I say this in conclusion, Mr. Speaker. Our railways, the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National, are under an obligation to carry out their side of the bargain and we, as members of the House of Commons, must insist that if we are to keep to our side of the bargain the railways must' fulfil theirs.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS, AIR CANADA PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill has now been the subject of extensive debate. I gather there has been some disposition on the part of certain mem-

DEBATES	December 3# 1969
bers of the government, and in particular the government house leader, to question the necessity and propriety of debating this matter to the extent that it has been debated. But, I think, to fail to recognize the need for this debate is to fail to recognize its significance.
I think that there are some significant aspects and implications which arise out of the debate that has taken place. I think, in the first place, that it of course demonstrated the very obvious factor of the importance of the transportation industry to Canada and the importance of the railway industry in particular. I think the second point of significance to be noted is that the contributions that have been made from all comers of this House indicate that in fact there is some considerable degree of discontent with the service that has been provided by the railways of this country, including the CNR company with which we are dealing today. I think the third point of significance that should be noted is, in fact, that there is an anomaly in our transportation structure and in the workings of the railway industry in Canada today which is borne out by the fact that we have two major railway companies supposedly competing with each other in some areas of operation, but each in fact is in the other's way thus making it every difficult to provide the type of efficient, economical service which is so necessary if we are to operate the Canadian economy on the best possible basis. Of course, I think this leads to the logical conclusion and to the point that has been made by this party in this House on more than one occasion, namely, the necessity to nationalize and bring into public ownership the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
Today, Mr. Speaker, we are of course dealing with the operations and capital budget of Canadian National Railways. There is no need to go into the history of the Canadian National Railways at this time. The fact is that the railway was born when a reluctant government took over a number of bankrupt railway operations, bankruptcies which were the result of mistakes of government policy, in large measure, in the years prior to the 1920's. The government and Canadian National Railways have had to bear ever since the burden imposed as a result of errors of Canadian governments and Canadian public policy.
For many years when Canadian National Railways operated as a publicly owned enterprise there was something of an attitude of
December 3, 1969	COMMONS
disconsolate toleration towards it as a public enterprise. The railway was really something you could not do much about; you had to put up with it and operate it as best you could, while at the same time allowing ample scope for its competitor, the CPR, to have its own way in policy and operations. However, throughout the years it became apparent that as a result of the dedication of certain leaders in the Canadian National and the faithful service of many of its employees, the railway company was able to counteract some of the handicaps it worked under and some of the attitudes which were evident in government throughout the years. The result has been that over a period of years we have witnessed the development of a first-rate railway system in Canada.
I think the CNR rightly deserves the tribute of operating a first-rate railway system. It has proved beyond doubt that a publicly owned enterprise can be operated efficiently, in the public interest and to the benefit of the entire Canadian economy. This railway system was developed out of the salvage of the bankrupt systems to which I referred, in spite of the reluctance of governments throughout the years, in spite of debt loads which were foisted on the railway system and in spite of the political influence of the CPR. The CNR today is a first-rate railway system of which all Canadians can be proud. It has deficiencies, some of which I will deal with in a few minutes. But it is the leader in the transportation industry and transportation systems of this country and is in the forefront in technological developments involved in many areas of its operations. Its service has been generally good, although some questions could be asked about its rates, rate policy and freight rates in particular. Despite its freight rate policies throughout the years, its attitude has been one of providing service to people. For that it deserves tribute, and in that it stands sharply contrasted with its competitor, the Canadian Pacific Railway.
This contrast has been demonstrated most clearly in the CNR attitude towards passenger business. While there are some specific points of criticism that I could make regarding Canadian National Railway passenger operations, at the same time I think it can be said that the CNR has recognized that it is a publicly-owned railway system which has a responsibility to carry people as well as goods. In this, as I mentioned, it is sharply contrasted with the attitude of the CPR which now states that it wants to get out of
DEBATES	1561
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada the passenger business. We note, of course, the applications which have been made to the Canadian Transport Commission to discontinue most of the remaining few passenger operations in which the CPR is engaged. Of course, there are some members in this House who are quite suspicious of what the government is doing in this regard.
I might just mention here, Mr. Speaker, that I received, and I presume some hon. members received as well, a letter from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company recently. The letter in my hand was addressed to me at the House of Commons and in part reads as follows:
Considerable public attention has been focused on the move by Canada's major railways in seeking to be relieved of the burden of uneconomic
passenger-train services.
To explain this move, we have prepared the enclosed booklet which outlines in layman's terms the statutory process for examining the railway applications.
The letter tries to justify the application made by the CPR under the terms of the new Transportation Act. Mr. S. M. Gossage, VicePresident and Senior Executive Officer of the CPR at Montreal, was kind enough to enclose with the letter a little booklet which had been prepared by his company outlining why the CPR was making application to discontinue its passenger operations.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
It seems quite clear, Mr. Speaker, that Canadian Pacific Railway Company let the cat out of the bag when it sent this letter because, while it has some appearances of being a rather generous offer of doing whatever could be done to help those people who may be protesting the move made by that railway, it is pretty clear evidence that what the CPR is looking for is to get its fingers into the till of the Canadian public treasury. It wants to get the benefit of subsidies provided under the National Transportation Act for so-called uneconomic operations. A good many of us will be having quite a bit to say about that during the coming weeks as we examine the costing methods of the CPR and examine the discrepancies between the accounting methods of the CPR and those which have been established by the Canadian Transport Commission.
It is also rather ironic, Mr. Speaker, that we are now dealing with this application by the CPR to abandon virtually all of its passenger services when one considers some of the advertising by that railway. In particular, I draw Your Honour's attention to one CPR
1562	COMMONS
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada advertisement which I am sure every hon. member in this House has seen. I refer to the advertisement in which they feature, as the main part of their theme, the phrase, "Serving you in so many ways".
If the CPR gets its way, and if in fact these applications are granted, I think that theme will no longer be valid, if it ever did have validity. Certainly, the CPR will have to change a good deal of its advertising program if in fact these applications are granted by the Canadian Transport Commission.
We might also note the record of the CPR with regard to providing boxcars for grain. This is of particular interest to my constituents and, indeed, the whole province of Saskatchewan. Generally, the services provided by the CPR have been of a much poorer standard and quality than those provided by the CNR. Here again, I think the CNR is to be commended on at least some aspects of its attempts at programs to provide boxcars for the movement of grain to the elevators in western Canada. They have at least made an attempt to be of service to the people.
There is also a contrast between the approach of the CNR and CPR in dealing with the matter of branch line abandonment. If one goes back over the history of this particular matter, it can be seen from the time of the early 1960's that the CNR did take a responsible attitude in dealing with this question. One might disagree with some of their points, but nevertheless their attitude and approach had some degree of responsibility. They attempted to inform governments and people of what they were going to do and of their long range plans. This was in sharp contrast to the CPR which attempted to play all of its cards close to its chest and start the ball rolling to carry out a massive program of branch line abandonment in order to increase the profits that the CPR would receive.
I have already made reference to the recent applications by both the CNR and the other railway company to abandon passenger services. This, of course, comes within the scope of our consideration of this bill because it does, after all, deal with investments to be made by the railway companies in facilities and equipment.
I have noted the recent applications with respect to Regina in particular. At present the city of Regina is served by the main line of the CPR. There is one remaining passenger service to that city, namely The Canadian. On the other hand, the CNR passenger operation 
DEBATES	December 3, 1969
to Regina consists of a rail-liner connection with the CNR main line at Saskatoon. This is of considerable value for westbound passengers and passengers coming from the west who are able to travel on the CNR main line as far as Saskatoon. The schedules are then set up so that passengers may transfer to the rail-liner going to Regina. However, in a few minutes I intend to say something about the inadequacy of service for eastbound passengers who wish to use the CNR.
In looking at the various applications which were filed, particularly by the CNR, one notes that in fact the railways have not made an attempt to keep up with the needs of the times by introducing new modes and variations of service, for passengers when it became apparent that the old modes, which performed a very useful function at one time, were no longer adequate for the needs of people. One obvious example which comes to my mind is the Winnipeg-Churchill run of the CNR. According to schedules of the CNR, that railway still operates basically the same type of passenger train from Winnipeg to The Pas, and from there on to northern Manitoba points, as it has operated for years. The service has not varied very much. The service which is overnight, goes from Winnipeg through Dauphin, Kamsack, or Swan River, up to Hudson Bay and on to The Pas, and has been virtually the same for years. Of course, it is obvious that the CNR is losing money on this service. They claim that in 1968 their loss for this particular service, extending right up to Churchill, amounted to approximately $3.3 million. I am not in a position to quarrel with those figures. I believe they have some validity and they have to be taken into account by the railway in making its decisions regarding future operations.
Have the railways given adequate and serious consideration to alternatives in terms of services that might be provided? For instance, have they considered the possibility of making a main line connection from Melville north to Yorkton, Canora, Hudson Bay, then on to The Pas and thus having the connection to the north made with its main line train at Melville, Saskatchewan, a city in which I used to live. This city certainly has very adequate railway facilities and could act as a terminal point for this particular train service.
I am not suggesting that points such as Dauphin, Kamsack and Swan River should be left without train service. If my suggestion were accepted, it would certainly be much
December 3, 1969

easier to have a train operating out of Melville to northern points on the one hand and a rail-liner service provided to people living in the Dauphin, Swan River and Kamsack areas of Manitoba and Saskatchewan on the other hand. I have not heard whether the railways have given serious consideration to such a possibility.
I have certainly found in my own contacts with the railways that the CNR in particular has been quite prepared to innovate and develop new services when they have been shown that they have a good chance of success and that they are needed by the public. At the same time there has also been a reluctance, and a rather queer sort of reasoning on occasion, when turning down proposals for new services. I will give an example of that in a few minutes when dealing with passenger train service by the CNR to the city of Regina.
I have already made reference to the attitude of the CNR with respect to its branch line operations and its main line operations. In considering the question of passenger service, I find it rather difficult to understand why the CNR withdrew so many of its passenger train services on branch lines just prior to the introduction of its new fare plans and of its new passenger programs.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
In particular I should like to cite one example with which I am quite familiar. This is the CN line which runs from Winnipeg, through Dauphin, Kamsack, Humboldt, on to Saskatoon; and from there it would either take the route to Calgary or to North Bat-tleford and Edmonton. The line running through Dauphin, Kamsack and Humboldt is the old main line of the Canadian Northern Railway. For years passenger trains Nos. 9 and 10 operated on those lines. I have had many occasions to make use of this service, as have other members of my family. It was a very popular service. However, as time passed the extent to which it was used diminished as a result of the schedules that were in use, as well as for a number of other reasons including continually rising fares.
Then in 1962 or 1963 this service, which had been in operation for many years, finally came to an end and was withdrawn by the railway. Shortly after this operation was closed out, the company introduced its new fare plan, the red, white and blue plan. It seems to me that if this new plan had been
DEBATES	1563
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada put into operation at a time when services such as the one to which I have just referred were still in operation, one would have found that the movement away from the use of passenger train services on lines such as this would have been stemmed, and this would have contributed to the maintenance of the passenger train operations carried on by the railway.
I should like to deal very briefly with the specific situation faced by my own city of Regina. I have the honour of representing part of the city as well as some of the rural area surrounding it. As I have said previously, the city of Regina is served by the CPR main line. As the House knows, the CPR has served notice that it wishes to discontinue its sole remaining passenger train service to that city. I imagine the company will be able to cite figures to show that the service is not being used much by the people of Regina, and this may well be the case.
However, I think the company should also understand why the service is not used very much by the people of Regina. If one looks at the hours when the train arrives at and leaves Regina, one will see why the service is so inadequate. The No. 1 train, the Canadian, coming from the east, leaves Winnipeg at eleven o'clock in the evening and arrives at Regina at six o'clock in the morning. The time of arrival in that case is a reasonable one. But when it comes to the return trip from Regina going east, the Canadian leaves Regina at 2.05 in the morning. The first major city along the line, with apologies to Brandon and some other intermediate centres, is Winnipeg, where it arrives at 9.05 in the morning. I suggest that the hour of 2.05 in the morning is not going to entice people to use this particular service.
In 1965, when the CPR made application to the Board of Transport Commissioners, as it then was, to discontinue the operation of its second trans-continental train which passed through Regina, the Dominion, I had occasion to make a presentation to the board when it held hearings in the city of Regina. I listened to the evidence given at the hearing very closely, and at that time the CPR gave assurances that they planned to continue operating the Canadian for a long, long time. It seems that that long, long time is now coming to an end, if the latest CPR application means what it says.
I think this is a further illustration why this railway system, which operates in competition, at least to some degree, with the pub-

December 3, 1969
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada licly owned railway system, cannot be relied on to provide the type of service that is required by the people of Canada. Its latest application is just one more piece of evidence to support the stand that I and my colleagues have taken for many years, namely that the Canadian Pacific and its associated companies should be put under public ownership.
In regard to CNR connections to Saskatoon, the schedules are designed to offer services that connect with the mainline trains. When the schedules for the fall and winter of 196970 were recently published, I wrote to the president of the Canadian National Railways to inform him of my views concerning the introduction of these schedules at the end of October. I wrote to Mr. N. J. MacMillan, president of the CNR, under date October 27 in regard to this matter, and in my letter I said:
I must say that I was very disappointed at the inadequacy of service provided to Regina. The only passenger train connection with the CN mainline is through the rail liner service between Regina and Saskatoon. I note that the rail liner schedules have been developed to coincide with transcontinental train arrivals and departures from Saskatoon. The result is an atrocious service so far as Regina is concerned.
I think it is totally unacceptable that the only rail liner service from Regina to Saskatoon and Prince Albert should be a train that leaves Regina at 6.00 o'clock in the morning in order to make a connection with the westbound supercontinental shortly after 9.00 a.m. The second train from Regina to Saskatoon leaves Regina at 7.50 in the evening and arrives in Saskatoon at 10.55 in time to meet the eastbound Panorama shortly after 11.00 o'clock. The rail liner then arrives in Prince Albert at
I.	45 a.m.
On the return trip, I note that one rail liner leaves Prince Albert at 6.55 a.m., meets transcontinental trains in Saskatoon shortly after 9.00 a.m., and arrives in Regina at 1.00 p.m. The second train leaves Prince Albert at 8.45 p.m., meets transcontinental trains in Saskatoon near
II.	00 p.m., and arrives in Regina at 2.30 a.m.
I recognize that some of these schedules have to be developed in conjunction with transcontinental train time tables, and thus there are some limitations. However, it seems to me that one solution to the problem of making adequate connections with Regina has not been fully explored. This would involve a train connection between Regina and Melville with a possibility of tie-ins with other points. Would it not be possible to have trains that would carry a sleeper for transfer at Melville which could provide much better service that would be well patronized and which would be much easier than trying to make every rail liner schedule between Regina and Saskatoon fit the transcontinental time tables?
Then, I suggested to the president of the CNR that I would be interested in having his views on this subject, and that I would

be quite prepared to explore the possibilities of this type of service with his officials.
Subsequently, I received a reply from the president of the CNR. After thanking me for my letter, he wrote:
Concerning the through sleeping car operation via Melville, please be assured that this has been studied thoroughly but would not be viable due to insufficient traffic. During August 1969 an average of less than five passengers daily were ticketed from Regina to eastern Canada. The cost to CN of operating a 2 or 3-car train between Melville-Regina would be very high compared to the revenue gained, even with a substantial increase in traffic. A less expensive Railiner operation on this route would not be practical because of the night operation necessary to connect with Trains 1-2, Super Continental, at Melville.
He then went on to indicate there would be some operating problems, and finally he gave me some information about the number of passengers that originated at Regina, classified on the basis of destination area. He indicated that 44 per cent of the passengers from Regina had as their destination local stations between Regina and Saskatoon, Prince Albert and Saskatoon, or Prince Albert and connections beyond.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
At the same time 42 per cent of the passengers originating at Regina had as their destination connections with western Canada; that is, points on the CNR main line or adjacent to it from Saskatoon on west. However, passengers to eastern Canada, including Winnipeg, amounted to only 14 per cent of the passengers originating at Regina. This figure applied to the month of August, 1969. There are just a couple of comments I would like to make in that respect.
First of all, it seems to me that the President of the CNR has proven by the statistics he presented to me the need for improved service from Regina to eastern Canadian points. I suggest to him and those responsible that the reason there is such a small proportion of people who commence their travels to eastern Canada by rail at Regina is the poor service provided by the CNR to the east. I suggest that if in fact there were a better type of service to the east we would find a very substantial increase in the volume of that classification of traffic.
On the other hand, the President of the CNR also pointed out problems involved in operating a train between Regina and Melville, a run of some 90 miles or more by rail. He suggested a two or three car train would be quite expensive and that a rail-liner oper-
December 3, 1969
ation would not work very well because it would make connections at Melville during the night time hours, which would pose some rather obvious difficulties, as I understood his letter. It seems to me this is an example of the type of lack of imagination one sees on the part of the railways from time to time, to which I made reference earlier.
It seems to me it should be quite within the scope of the imagination of CNR officials to devise a plan whereby, if in fact it is not economic to operate a two or three car train between Regina and Melville as the president points out, it would be possible to operate a rail-liner service from Regina to Melville and perhaps points beyond, then provide for sleeping car service originating at Melville. The passengers could transfer at Melville at some reasonable hour in the evening to the sleeper that would be stationed there.
I suggest this service would be quite heavily patronized by people not only from Regina but also people living along the line at intermediate points and customers from Melville, Yorkton and portions of eastern Saskatchewan. It seems to me this is a rather obvious step that should be taken by the railway if in fact it is going to follow through with its policy of attempting to exploit all worthwhile possibilities of improving passenger traffic in various parts of Canada.
Thus, we see many examples of lousy timetables, which are responsible for the small amount of passenger patronage of the railway lines. I think the example I have cited in respect of the service between Regina and Saskatoon should be quite adequate to illustrate this. Certainly, the hours that these trains operate will not attract as many people as might possibly want to travel by rail. I have also cited the situation in respect of those people who wish to use CN services for travel to eastern Canada.
I also noted in the list of applications submitted by the CNR and CPR a number of other passenger runs they are proposing to abandon. I do not intend to discuss each one of them because I am not personally familiar with many. I did note one particular example which I think should be drawn to the attention of this House. Both the CNR and the CPR applied for abandonment of their Calgary-Edmonton runs. It seems to me that this is complete nonsense. Both railways claim a substantial loss on their operations between Calgary and Edmonton. I fail to understand why this need be the case. Possibly one alter-
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada native which should be examined is the provision of a joint service between Calgary and Edmonton. This might possibly deal with the deficit problems which both railways allege they face.
Still more attention needs to be paid, in terms of passenger train service, to the provision of adequate service to a number of small points along the main line of the CNR. I could cite a number of examples in my own constituency. The Canadian National Railways main line crosses my constituency in the northern part, and there are a number of communities located along that main line within the boundaries of my constituency. There are also a number of urban areas there, each one with approximately 500 people. I refer specifically to the communities of Kelliher, Lestock and Punnichy. There are a number of other nearby communities. In addition, there is the rural population which makes use of these communities.
For some time now there has been no provision in the Canadian National Railways schedules for passenger stops along these lines. It seems to me this is one matter which should be looked into. I recognize some of the problems in making frequent stops along any particular line, but when revenue business is available, certainly in the long run it would be to the benefit of the railways to ensure the provision of an adequate level of service to these communities as well as to the larger centres across Canada. Thus, I think it is important that we consider the future of passenger train business. I certainly urge the Canadian National Railways to continue its operations on the basis which it has in terms of following the principle of providing service for travelling people as well as for the transportation of goods. The CNR is in a very good position to show up the CPR and its complete lack of regard for the needs of people.
At the time the Canadian Transport Commission hears the applications of the Canadian Railway companies, I hope and trust it will pay adequate attention to the applications made by the railways, the CPR in particular, and the accounting and costing procedures used in reporting some of the deficits cited in their applications and public reports. It is important that we do not just assume the attitude of one who picks up the tab whenever the railways report they are not making a profit on some of their passenger operations. It is important that we look at their accounting methods and the figures they submit to

December 3, 1969
1566	COMMONS
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada the Transport Commission very closely in order to make certain we are in fact not simply picking up that tab when there is no justification for doing so.
Another matter of interest and concern to the city of Regina is air service. This of course also comes within the scope of this bill. Regina is served by Air Canada operations, and a good many of their services are excellent and commendable. There have been .complaints from time to time about the inadequacy of services to eastern Canada. Over the past year and a half I have had the opportunity, as a result of facilities made available to members of Parliament, to make use of Air Canada services in travelling between Ottawa and my constituency. I have done so in looking after the needs of my constituents and carrying out my duties as a member of Parliament.
Very often I have found that Air Canada service is quite good. I have one complaint, and that is that there is no direct service between Regina and eastern Canadian points.
I made representations about this matter when I made my first speech in the House of Commons on September 23, 1968.
Subsequently I wrote to the former Minister of Transport and Air Canada, drawing to their attention the representations I had made in respect of direct air connections between Regina and eastern Canada. I received a very nice reply from the Acting President of Air Canada in which he informed me that it was the intention of Air Canada to introduce a new direct air connection between Regina and Eastern Canada in the spring of 1969. He hoped that I would have the patience to wait until this new service could be inaugurated.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Well, I did have the patience to wait and the new service was introduced. It was used by many people. The occupancy rate was very high during the summer season of 1969. But to the surprise of everyone in the city of Regina who was interested in the matter, and to my surprise, when the fall schedule of Air Canada was published it was found they had eliminated this direct connection between Regina and Toronto. A great deal of protest was made about the matter. Then Air Canada, for the first time, informed the people who made inquiries that their plan was to introduce this new service initially for the summer season only and that it would be introduced again in the spring of 1970. They
(Mr. Burton.]

Mr. Speaker, I shall not take too long, but I felt I should say something about this
December 3. 1969

bill. I was impressed by the comments made by several members, particularly the hon. member for Thunder Bay (Mr. Penner) who last evening made a plea on behalf of his constituency and talked about the people who want to protect their towns.
As we all know, Bill C-7 is supposed to provide funds for the financing of the CNR and Air Canada. Possibly it is because of my inexperience, but as a new member I wonder why such a bill is necessary. I am doubtful that it should be necessary for the CNR and Air Canada to come to the House of Commons with a bill requesting money that has already been spent. The reason for this is beyond me, but I will tag along with this procedure for another couple of years.
As members of parliament representing Canadians I think we must clamp down very seriously on the activities of the various modes of transportation. It certainly is high time we took a close look at the policies in respect of railways and transportation in general. There is no doubt that in certain parts of Canada, particularly in the east and in the west, transportation is vital and must be improved. It is difficult for me to believe that the only solution the railway companies can come up with is abandonment of service or restriction of service. The other day in a French newspaper I read how Japan had introduced rapid transportation services. I read also that France was introducing a new service to provide fast and efficient transportation for the public. In a growing country like Canada, apparently the only solution we have is abandonment of the whole passenger service because it does not pay. This is the reason I am very reluctant to give approval to this bill, although I imagine I will have to do so.
Every day we read in the press that more and more people are becoming afraid to drive on the highways. The number of fatalities on the highway is increasing. The figures are even greater than the casualty figures of the armed forces. I am convinced that if a proper service were provided the people definitely would use it. The trend today is for people to commute from the city to the fringe areas. They travel back and forth every day, some for short distances and some for longer distances. Some people travel on the week-ends while others do so on a day to day basis. In many instances, the railways do not provide any adequate service for the people. The trend today for people to work in the cities is
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada fine, because this is the only place they can find work; but they live outside the cities. These people do not wish to spend an hour travelling back and forth a couple of miles a day in their cars. Surely, we should be able to devise a much better and modem way of transportation. Of course, it is necessary that the schedules be such that they are suitable for the commuters. It is not good enough to have a train which departs at two o'clock in the afternoon and expect that train to accommodate the working class. This isi what is happening in some areas.
In Nova Scotia, for example, a train which travels from Halifax to Yarmouth leaves some time around noon. How can it be expected that the people will use this type of service? I am convinced that the Canadian people would patronize a good system. I believe the railways must come up with something new and that the Canadian Transport Commission must exercise its responsibilities in this regard. The Minister of Transport and members of this House, I suggest, also have a responsibility to see that a good, modern, efficient service is provided. We live in the year 1969. Men are going to the moon. Certainly modern technology could provide the means for a fast efficient service.
I might mention the ferry system operated by the Canadian National Railways and by the Canadian Pacific Railway between provinces like Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, and even between Nova Scotia and the state of Maine. Will these be cancelled also? This question is of concern to the people in my area. As we move into the 70's it is not good enough to accept the present railway system of transportation or the standards under which it is being operated. I am convinced that a proper handling of the railway company's finances and of the service would eradicate the deficits and make a system much more attractive to the public.

What else can the committee do with this bill but accept or reject it? It certainly cannot formulate policies in so far as transportation is concerned because the government does not usually accept the reports of standing committees, particularly of the Committee on Transport and Communications.
I should like to say in conclusion that we have to come up with a better solution than the abandonment of rail service. speechtext:
I want to take a few moments this afternoon to join my colleagues in this House in discussing Bill C-7, to authorize the provision of moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways system and Air Canada. I have been very interested in the remarks of many speakers who have taken part in the debate. They impressed on me the importance of the whole subject matter dealt with in the bill. Several days ago, the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) opened up in a non partisan manner a broad spectrum of problems facing transportation in Canada at present. These problems are likely to continue to face us in the future. A number of years ago I had the privilege of being a member of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. During that time we brought forth the bill setting up the Canadian Transport Commission. It was interesting at that time to listen to the discussions that took place with respect to the costing formula.
Although this matter has not been referred to recently, it continues to be one of the basic issues facing the commission in arriving at a decision with respect to applications for rail line abandonment. All this goes back to the MacPherson Royal Commission in the latter part of the 1950's when the Hon. M. N. MacPherson of Regina, who was recognized as one of the foremost authorities on transportation in Canada, brought in a very forthright report. During the discussions of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications
December 3, 1969	COMMONS
we discovered a thread of discontent running through all the evidence with respect to the transportation costing formula. The committee found that they could not accept the costing formula of the railway companies, and consequently an independent costing committee was set up made up of a group of experts on railway costing. It was a committee similar in type to the one working for the inter-state commerce commission in the United States. Nevertheless they brought in an independent report on the cost of railroading in Canada, and it so greatly differed from the costing formula used by the railroads that we were led to believe we would have to take another look at this, which we did. As a result the figures submitted by the railroads at that time were thrown out, and a compromise was adopted by your committee in arriving at certain costs.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
It was also laid down in the new act setting up the Canadian Transport Commission that there should be a group of experts within the commission whose job would be to decide on a costing formula that would be satisfactory both to the people of Canada and the railroads. It worries me to some extent to find that presently the CPR has decided to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada against the costing formula that has been adopted and is presently under consideration for use by the Canadian Transport Commission.
Here again we find another confrontation between the people of Canada, represented by the Canadian Transport Commission, and the railroads. They are disagreeing on what should be a proper costing formula. Therefore, we cannot arrive at any proper decision regarding the present host of applications for railway line abandonment. We cannot reach such a decision until we get agreement on the costing formula. This was the reason that last week I felt it necessary to suggest to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) that the government of Canada be represented by the best legal talent available before the Supreme Court of Canada in its hearings on the CPR appeal.
I am naturally concerned, like other hon. members, about the host of applications presently being made for rail line abandonment. As mentioned by many hon. members, transportation is the sinew of our economy, and the various modes of transportation, air, rail, automotive and bus are all interlocked. Rela-
